cards.text: The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers, and he wants them to know who they've got on their side. We have a high priest, Jesus the Son of God. Not a decent high priest. Not a pretty good one. A GREAT one.

cards.question: Jesus, our great high priest, has passed through somewhere. Where?
Since we have a great high priest like Jesus, what does the writer of Hebrews say we should do?

answers.text: Hold firmly to what we profess
Offer our gifts at the temple

cards.question: Jesus has passed through the heavens, so He is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses.

cards.text: Jesus is NOT the boss who's never worked one single shift up front. He was tempted in every way that we are.

cards.question: Jesus was tempted in every way that we are. How did it turn out?

cards.text: So what do we do with a high priest who knows what it's like down here? The writer says we approach the throne of grace.

cards.question: How does the writer of Hebrews say we should approach the throne of grace?
At the throne of grace, we may receive ___ and find grace to help us in our time of need.

cards.text: Confidence, friend. Not holding your breath like I did every time that junk drawer slid open. Now the writer pulls out the job description for every high priest, not just Jesus.

cards.question: Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God.
A high priest offers gifts and ___ for sins.

cards.text: Here's the upside of a high priest picked from regular people. He's able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided.

cards.question: Why is a high priest able to deal gently with the ignorant and misguided?

answers.text: He is subject to weakness himself
He was trained to be patient
The law orders him to be kind

cards.question: A high priest offers sacrifices only for the people's sins and never for his own.

cards.text: He's obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins too, right alongside the people's. And I get it, friend. I can't laugh at your burnt batch when MY tray is still smoking.
Back to that high priest job description. Being high priest is an honor. So how does a person end up with it?

cards.question: How does someone receive the honor of being high priest?

answers.text: He must be called by God

cards.question: Who does the writer of Hebrews name as a high priest called by God?
Christ took on Himself the glory of becoming a high priest.

cards.text: Christ was called, just like Aaron. He was called by the One who said to Him, "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father."

cards.question: In another passage, God says Christ will be a priest only for His lifetime on earth.

cards.text: God says, "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." That's Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abram (Genesis 14:18-19).
Now the writer looks back at Jesus' days on earth. He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears.

cards.question: Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from ___.
When Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears, He was heard. Why?
Although Jesus was a Son, He learned obedience from what He ___.

cards.text: Let that sit for a second. He was the Son, and He learned obedience through what He suffered.

cards.question: Having been made perfect, Jesus became the source of what?
Jesus is the source of eternal salvation only for the priests.

cards.text: And God designated Him high priest in the order of Melchizedek. Nobody's sliding THIS high priest into a junk drawer for a shinier model. Trust me, friend. I know how that one goes.

findings.problem: The opening card has five sentences. It also doesn't give the context the passage picks up from. Hebrews 4:14 starts with "Therefore," but the card never says what that follows.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: "He wants them to know who they've got on their side" states the writer's purpose as fact. Hebrews 4:14 doesn't say why the writer says this.

rule.text: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: "Only once a year" is about how often, but "With confidence" and "With our heads down" are about manner. The answers aren't the same kind of thing.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: "The job description for every high priest, not just Jesus" says Hebrews 5:1-3 applies to Jesus too. That would include offering sacrifices for his own sins (5:3), which 4:15 ("without sin") contradicts. The text only connects Christ to the calling part (5:4-5).

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke is about not laughing at someone else's mistake when you've made your own. That matches dealing gently because of your own weakness (5:2). It doesn't match the action this card tells, offering sacrifices for his own sins as well as the people's (5:3).

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The card only restates what card 15 just settled, that the high priest offers sacrifices for his own sins too. It adds nothing new from the passage.
This story card has three sentences. It isn't the walkthrough's opening card.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The right answer "Aaron brother of Moses" states a fact from outside the passage (Exodus 4:14). The card gives no reference for it and cites only Hebrews 5:4.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The card tells a fact from Genesis 14:18-19 and puts its reference in the text. The card's "verses" field lists only Hebrews 5:6.
findings.question: When a story card uses an outside fact with its reference, should the reference stay in the card text, or go in the "verses" field too?

findings.problem: The card only repeats what card 11 just asked, that He learned obedience from what He suffered. It doesn't move the passage forward.
No card tells who the eternal salvation is for, "all who obey Him" (Hebrews 5:9). The false statement only rules out "only for the priests," so the baker leaves without this key detail.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Most of stop 2's story cards (1, 5, 7, 8, 12) are plain retelling with no humor. The only joke in the stop is on the last card, so the stop reads like a nice dad being pleasant, not laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
